hints.title: Two-Tier Social Network Association
hints.text: A user is a second-degree follower if they follow at least one person and also possess at least one follower themselves.

hints.title: Group Count with Subquery Membership
hints.text: Group by followee to count their incoming followers, filtering for users who also appear in the follower column.

hints.title: Second Degree Blueprint
hints.text: select followee as follower, count(distinct follower) as num from Follow where followee in (select follower from Follow) group by followee order by follower asc.

hints.title: Complete Implementation
hints.text:
```mysql
SELECT followee AS follower, COUNT(DISTINCT follower) AS num
FROM Follow
WHERE followee IN (SELECT follower FROM Follow)
GROUP BY followee
ORDER BY follower ASC;
```

variables: N: number of records in Follow table
complexity.notes: Subquery lookup and grouped aggregation executes in linear-logarithmic time.
complexity.whyNaiveFails: Cartesian self-joins generate redundant cross-product rows before grouping.
complexity.spaceTimeTradeoff: Semi-join membership IN isolates qualifying users without row duplication.
complexity.interviewerExpectation: Correctly identifying that the user must appear in both follower and followee roles.

SELECT followee AS follower, COUNT(DISTINCT follower) AS num
FROM Follow
WHERE followee IN (SELECT follower FROM Follow)
GROUP BY followee
ORDER BY follower ASC;

import pandas as pd

def second_degree_follower(follow: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    followers_set = set(follow['follower'])
    filtered = follow[follow['followee'].isin(followers_set)]
    res = filtered.groupby('followee')['follower'].nunique().reset_index()
    res.columns = ['follower', 'num']
    return res.sort_values(by='follower')
solutions.approach: Pandas Set Membership and Grouped Nunique
